title: How to Approach LLD Problems ?
summary: A no-fluff method for LLD interviews: clarify scope, model nouns, lock contracts, drive behavior, then stress extensibility and concurrency.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **LLD is not drawing boxes. It is choosing where behavior lives so a new requirement changes one class, not five.** If your design cannot absorb `cancel`, `discount`, `priority`, or `concurrent booking` without a rewrite, you failed — even if the code compiles. Every decision you make is a bet on what will change.
What LLD actually tests

Low Level Design is the translation of vague product requirements into **runnable object structure**: classes, interfaces, fields, method signatures, and who calls whom. The interviewer gives you something deliberately underspecified — parking lot, elevator, movie booking, rate limiter — and watches how you turn nouns into responsibilities and verbs into contracts. They do not grade you on syntax perfection. They grade you on three things: did you scope the problem before modeling it, did you put state and behavior in the right owner, and did you leave seams where change is cheap. A good LLD answer compiles in the head, handles the happy path cleanly, names what happens on conflict and failure, and can explain *why* `ParkingLot` does not calculate `Price` itself.

This is different from data structures and from high-level design, and confusing them is why most candidates stall. Data structures asks: what is the fastest algorithm for a fixed contract. High-level design asks: how do machines cooperate under load. LLD asks: what *should the contract be* and who enforces it. That means ambiguity is the test, not an accident. When the prompt says “design a parking lot,” there is no correct class list. There is only a defensible decomposition: `Vehicle` vs `Spot` vs `Ticket` vs `EntryPanel` vs `PricingStrategy`, with clear ownership of allocation, payment, and concurrency. If you jump to code without fixing scope, actors, and core use cases, you will model the wrong system well.
The mechanism: a tight loop, in this order

The order is the method. Clarify first because every entity you invent before scope is rework. Identify entities second because nouns bound the problem. Fix public contracts third because method signatures force you to decide who knows what. Only then do you wire interactions and object creation. Concurrency, persistence, and extensibility come last as stress tests, not starting points. Do it backwards — start with a database schema or `synchronized` everywhere — and you lock in a shape before you know the behavior. The trade-off is explicit: five minutes of questions feels slow, but it prevents fifteen minutes of refactoring dead code in front of an interviewer. Speed comes from discipline, not typing faster.

blocks.title: LLD delivery loop
blocks.caption: Run this loop, do not skip steps.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Clarify scope and use cases] --> B[Identify entities and owners]
  B --> C[Define contracts: public methods]
  C --> D[Wire interactions and creation]
  D --> E[Stress: extension + concurrency + failures]
  E -->|requirement changes| C

blocks.text: Trade-offs: every principle costs you something

blocks.caption: No principle is free. Name the cost when you use it.
rows: Abstraction via interfaces
Swap implementations, test in isolation
More files, indirection, harder to trace for a trivial problem
Composition over inheritance
No fragile base class, behavior can be mixed at runtime
More wiring, explicit delegation boilerplate
Strict SOLID / full patterns
Clean extension points
Over-engineering; 45 minutes dies to ceremony
Single manager / God service
Fast to write, easy to demo
All change funnels to one file; merge conflicts and untestable logic
Pessimistic locking everywhere
Obviously safe
Kills throughput, hides the real invariant you should have modeled

blocks.text: Interviewers listen for this accounting. Saying “I will use Strategy for pricing” is junior. Saying “I am pulling pricing into a `PricingStrategy` because rules change per vehicle type and time of day, and the cost is one extra interface — worth it here, not worth it for a fixed flat fee” is senior. The same logic applies to factories, observers, and thread-safety. Do not apply a principle because you memorized it. Apply it because a specific future change is likely and the seam is cheap now but expensive later. If you cannot name the change you are buying insurance against, do not buy it. That is the difference between design and decoration.
How it fails in production — and what the interviewer smells

Bad LLD fails the same three ways in production and in the interview: wrong owner, missing invariant, and hidden coupling. Wrong owner means `ParkingLot.park(vehicle)` does spot search, payment, ticket printing, and notification — so adding EV charging or dynamic pricing touches everything. Missing invariant means two threads book the last spot because “check then act” was never atomic — the code looked correct single-threaded. Hidden coupling means `Question` directly updates `User.reputation` and sends email, so you cannot test voting without a mail server. The interviewer does not need to run your code to see this. They look at method sizes, at who mutates whom, and at whether creation logic is scattered across callers with `new` everywhere.

items: **Symptom: God class.** One `Manager` with 20 methods and all the `if-else` on type. Any new vehicle type or discount rule edits the same file.
**Symptom: Anemic model.** Data classes with getters plus a `Util` that does everything. Behavior lives nowhere, so invariants live nowhere.
**Symptom: Inheritance explosion.** `CarSpot`, `BikeSpot`, `EVCarSpot`, `HandicappedEVCarSpot`. You modeled variation with subclassing instead of composition.
**Symptom: Check-then-act race.** `if spot.isFree() then spot.assign()` without atomic claim. Passes demo, double-books under load.
**Symptom: No seam for creation.** Callers call `new ConcretePricing()` directly. Swapping a rule means editing every caller instead of one factory.

blocks.text: What good structure looks like

This shape wins because responsibility is placed where change is expected. `ParkingLot` owns the lifecycle — issue and close tickets — but it does not own *how* a spot is chosen or *how* price is computed. Those vary independently, so they get interfaces. State that must stay consistent (`active` tickets, spot occupancy) lives behind two methods, `park` and `unpark`, which are the only places that need atomicity. The trade-off is two extra abstractions for a toy problem, but that is exactly the point: you are showing you know where the system will bend. An interviewer can now ask “add EV priority” or “add hourly cap” and you change `SpotAllocation` or `PricingStrategy` without touching `Ticket`. If you had inlined pricing with `if vehicle == CAR`, that follow-up becomes surgery.
Patterns: use three, ignore the rest

You need Strategy, Observer, and Factory / Builder for 90% of LLD rounds. Strategy isolates rules that change — pricing, ranking, eviction, rate limiting. Observer decouples side effects — notify, reputation update, audit log — from core state change, so voting does not depend on email. Factory centralizes `new` so variation in creation does not leak to callers. Everything else — Singleton, Adapter, Decorator, State — is situational; mention it only when the problem demands it. The common failure is pattern-first design: forcing AbstractFactory into a 30-minute elevator problem. That signals you design from vocabulary, not from pressure. Better to write clean composition and let the interviewer name the pattern than to announce patterns you do not need. Composition plus clear interfaces beats a textbook diagram every time.

blocks.title: Prefer composition
blocks.caption: Variation via delegation, not subclass explosion.

blocks.text: How to run 45 minutes without running out of time

items.title: 0-5 min: Pin scope
items.text: List actors, 3-5 core use cases, and explicit non-goals. Agree on concurrency, persistence, and whether to code or diagram. Write it down; do not keep it in your head.

items.title: 5-10 min: Nouns and owners
items.text: Extract entities, kill duplicates. For each, state its single responsibility in one line. If you cannot, the entity is wrong. Decide what you will NOT model.

items.title: 10-20 min: Contracts before bodies
items.text: Write class shells with public methods and signatures only. Argue about parameters and return types. Who returns Optional vs throws? Who owns the ID? This is the design.

items.title: 20-32 min: One vertical slice
items.text: Implement the hardest flow end-to-end — e.g., park then unpark with payment — not every helper. Show state transitions and invariant enforcement, not getters and setters.

items.title: 32-40 min: Stress it
items.text: Walk a follow-up: cancel, extend, double-book, or new rule. Show where it plugs in. Add atomic claim or lock at the narrowest scope, not around the whole manager.

items.title: 40-45 min: Trade-offs out loud
items.text: State what you simplified and what breaks next. Memory, extensibility, thread-safety — pick two honestly. Interviewers promote candidates who know what they sacrificed.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that kill you

items: **More classes equals better design.** No — each class must own an invariant or a variation. Five empty data holders plus a util is worse than two honest classes.
**UML completeness matters.** It does not. A half-drawn diagram with correct ownership beats a perfect diagram with wrong behavior placement.
**You must write fully working code.** You must write *convincing* code: correct contracts, one working flow, and explicit handling of conflicts. Boilerplate can be stubbed if you say so.
**One big file is fine for speed.** It is not. It tells the interviewer you cannot see boundaries. Split by responsibility even on a whiteboard; the overhead is the signal.
**Concurrency means `synchronized` on everything.** That signals panic. Model the invariant first — single atomic claim — then guard only that critical section.
**Watching videos is preparation.** It is not. LLD is a writing skill. If you have not hand-written three designs under a timer, you have not prepared.

blocks.text: When to use each tool — and when to leave it out

blocks.caption: Apply pressure proportional to likely change.
rows: Interface + Strategy
Rule varies by type, time, or config — pricing, ranking, eviction
Rule is fixed and single — flat fee, FIFO with no exceptions
Observer / events
Side effects must not block core write — notifications, reputation
Only actor needs the result synchronously and there is one caller
Factory / Builder
Creation has branches or defaults callers should not know
One concrete type, no variation, test does not need a fake
Inheritance
True is-a with shared behavior and stable hierarchy — rarely
Variation is in capability or config — use composition with flags/strategies
Locks / concurrent maps
Check-and-claim must be atomic — booking, allocation
Single-threaded scope agreed; adding locks just adds noise

blocks.text: The meta-skill is balancing *extensible* against *YAGNI*. Over-abstract too early and you waste ten minutes interviewers wanted for behavior. Under-abstract and every follow-up — “now add coupons,” “now support trucks,” “now make it thread-safe” — forces edits across the codebase. The rule: abstract the axis the interviewer hinted will change, hard-code the rest. If they said “different vehicle types,” Strategy and Allocation earn their keep. If they never mentioned persistence, do not design tables. Say it explicitly: “I am keeping storage in-memory behind a `TicketStore` interface so we can swap it later without paying for it now.” That sentence shows judgment, which is what the round is actually scoring.

blocks.title: The trap to avoid
blocks.text: Do not start with getters, setters, and a database schema. Start with **who can break what**. If two threads can claim the same spot, or a cancel can leave money captured, your class list is irrelevant. Fix the invariant, then fix the classes.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence
blocks.text: “I scope use cases first, assign each behavior to a single owner, lock public contracts, implement one end-to-end flow, then show where extension and atomicity plug in — and I name what I deliberately left out.”
